newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Manuel's S.African budget has tough spending cuts.
newsitem.headline: Manuel's S.African budget has tough spending cuts.

text.p: South African Finance Minister Trevor Manuel on Wednesday proposed expenditure of 186.7 billion rand in a disciplined budget, slashing the real value of spending plans well below last year's level.
"This budget is a tough budget. It demands substantially more austerity from government than many of its forerunners have," Manuel told parliament in his budget address.
He added, however, that the government had not sacrificed its plan to transform South Africa's once white-ruled society and said poverty relief was a key focus of spending.
The expenditure budget was 6.1 percent higher than the revised figure for the financial year ending on March 31, but 2.4 percent lower than the projected 8.5 percent inflation rate for the period.

With revenue up 11 percent to 161.9 billion rand, the austere spending programme contributed to a reduction in the budget deficit to 4.0 percent in fiscal 1997/98 from an estimated 5.1 percent in the year to March 31.
State debt, housing and police were the main items increased in Manuel's budget with defence, down 667 million rand to 9.579 billion, the biggest loser.
"In this budget we make a substantial allocation to poverty relief. We invest in people through a significant reprioritisation of expenditures in favour of social development," he said.
Special allocations for transformation included 300 million for community-based poverty relief, an additional one billion rand for social welfare and 75 million rand for child support.
"This budget tells the story of a government determined to effect deep transformation and to live within its means."
Finance department officials said the cut in non-debt expenditure was the biggest ever proposed in recent South African history.

Debt servicing, up by 3.6 billion rand to 39.6 billion rand, was the biggest single item, but 80.4 billion rand, equivalent to 57 percent of non-debt expenditure, was allocated directly to the country's nine provincial governments for services including housing and education.
Manuel said the 40.2 billion rand combined national and provincial budget for education comprised the biggest single functional item, at 21.3 percent of total expenditure.
The 20.2 billion rand health budget comprised 10.7 percent of total expenditure and social security, at 18.4 billion rand, comprised 9.8 percent of total expenditure.
Announcing a total 29.6 billion rand budget for police, defence and justice, Manuel said: "A safe and peaceful society is essential for democracy and economic development."

He said the 9.6 billion rand defence budget was 6.5 percent down on the figure for 1996/97 and represented a cut in the defence budget to 1.5 percent of gross domestic product in fiscal 1997/98 from 4.5 percent in 1989/90.
Police battling a post-apartheid crime wave cited as a deterrent by many foreign investors were given a 20.6 percent boost to 11.9 billion rand.
Manuel set aside 4.875 billion rand for the completion of a programme agreed with public sector unions for the improvement of civil service employment packages.
